opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is the pre-training data. Everyone is pre-training on more or less the same data, which is essentially the internet, and so the models end up being quite similar. Pre-training is this very blunt, very powerful instrument: you take all the data, you train a big neural net on it, and what comes out reflects that data. If everyone uses roughly the same data and roughly the same recipe, you shouldn't be surprised that the models end up resembling each other.

Where you start to see differences is in what comes after, in the RL and post-training. That's where people make different choices about what environments to train on, what to optimize for, and what kind of behavior they want. But even there, a lot of companies are looking at the same evals and the same benchmarks, so there's a pull toward convergence there too.

If you think about it from the perspective of people, humans are very diverse. Even two people who grew up in similar circumstances end up thinking quite differently, because they had different experiences, made different choices, and learned different things along the way. Today's models don't really have that. They don't learn continually from their own unique experience. So in a sense, the lack of diversity is a symptom of how we train them right now.

I think if you want real diversity, the kind where different models genuinely approach a problem from different angles, the kind that would make something like multi-agent debate or self-play actually productive, you need to find ways of creating it on purpose. You could try to induce it through different post-training, but I suspect the more fundamental answer will come when models learn more like people do: from their own experience, over time, in their own particular ways. Then diversity becomes natural rather than something you have to engineer.

r001.rationale: It says models are trained on essentially the same internet data and therefore end up similar.

r002.rationale: It identifies differing choices in RL and post-training as where models begin to diverge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the lack of diversity is actually one of the more revealing things about the current moment, because it tells you something about where the ideas are coming from. Everyone is training on more or less the same data, with more or less the same recipe, and the recipe works, so there is very little pressure to deviate from it. When something works, you scale it. That is the lesson of the past decade, and people learned it very well. Perhaps too well.

But I think there is a deeper reason, which is that the pre-training paradigm is in some sense convergent. If you take a large enough model and you ask it to predict the next token on the entire internet, the thing it learns is largely determined by the data, not by you. Two labs with different cultures and different people will end up with models that are strangely similar, because they are both approximations of the same underlying distribution. The model is a compression of the world as it appears in text, and the world is the same for everyone. So the diversity you would normally expect from different research groups gets washed out.

And I would say the models themselves are not very diverse internally either. They have a kind of flatness to them. They know a great deal, they can do a great many things, but they have the character of a very well-read generalist rather than many distinct minds. I think this is a consequence of the objective. You are rewarding the model for being the average of everyone who wrote on the internet, and then with RL you push it toward some notion of being helpful, and that also tends to be a single target.

So the question I find more interesting is not why the models are so similar now, but what would make them different. I think the answer is that we have mostly exhausted what pre-training by itself can give you, and the next phase will be about the research ideas again rather than just the scaling. And once ideas matter again, you will see divergence, because different people will have different ideas about how a system should learn, how it should generalize from less data, how it should have something like taste or judgment rather than just knowledge. That is where I expect the diversity to come back. Not in the data, but in the learning itself.

r001.rationale: It says models use “more or less the same data” and that next-token pretraining on the internet makes them similar.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning pushes models toward a single target, contributing to similarity. It does not identify differences in RL training as a source of differentiation.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different things you could mean by diversity. You could mean that the models give similar answers, or that they have similar strengths and weaknesses. Those aren't necessarily the same phenomenon.

But the models are trained on very similar data, with very similar objectives. So perhaps it shouldn't be surprising that they end up being similar. The architectures differ in details, but the basic task is the same: learn to predict what comes next in text.

The interesting question is how much of that similarity is inevitable. If two models understand something correctly, you would expect them to agree. But if they make the same mistakes, that's more revealing. Is it because they saw the same data? Because the training procedure encourages the same shortcuts? Or because some things are intrinsically difficult to learn this way?

I would want to distinguish those possibilities before concluding that there's some fundamental lack of diversity.

r001.rationale: It says the models are trained on very similar data and suggests this helps explain why they end up similar.

r002.rationale: It mentions similar objectives and training procedures, but does not identify differences in reinforcement learning as a source of differentiation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that the models are trained on very similar data, with very similar objectives. So although the architectures and the details of training may differ, they’re all trying to discover the same underlying structure in language and in the world. It’s perhaps not so surprising that they arrive at similar answers.

But there are two different things you might mean by diversity. One is diversity of capability: do different models know different things or make different mistakes? The other is diversity of behavior: do they have different personalities, different ways of approaching a question? Post-training can make the second look very similar even if there are differences underneath.

The interesting question is how much of this convergence is inevitable. If there are a few particularly effective ways to learn from the data, you would expect convergence. If there are many equally effective ways, then perhaps the similarity tells us more about how similar our training methods still are.

r001.rationale: The response says the models are trained on “very similar data,” attributing their similarity partly to shared training data.

r002.rationale: It mentions post-training and training methods generally, but does not identify differences in reinforcement learning training as a source of model differentiation.
